newsitem.title: INDIA: Bombay stocks end mixed in roller-coaster ride.
newsitem.headline: Bombay stocks end mixed in roller-coaster ride.

text.p: ** (1005 GMT)- Bombay shares end little changed as
profit-taking caps four-day old rally
** Bombay index closes 0.72 pts at a provisional 4,029.27,
off 4,076.56 --intra-day high
** Crucial meeting of ruling United Front's steering
committee late evening on Monday to tackle expected rise
in prices of petroleum products weighs on market
** State Bank of India up 9.25 rupees at 327.75 after
stock enters no-delivery phase from Monday
** Tobacco giant ITC tumbles 53.25 rupees or 10 pct at
481.75 amid heavy volumes
Shares at Bombay exchanges closed little changed on Monday, capping a day of wild swings on a bout of profit-taking with market attention focussed on select stocks, dealers said.
"This is a healthy correction we have seen today," said Kuntal Shah, chief dealer at brokers D.T. Gandhi. "I am still bullish."
The marginal fall in the Bombay index snapped the market's four-day old rally, capping last week's five percent surge.
Shares which entered into a no-delivery phase cornered market attention, traders said.
Larsen & Toubro edged up 1.25 rupees to 239.75, Mahindra rose 18.0 to 396.0, Bajaj Auto added 17.75 to 912.50, SBI climbed 9.25 to 327.75 and Tata Tea gained 27.0 to 373.0.
A no-delivery benefits speculators, as it enables them to buy the shares without taking delivery for about a month.
"The correction in prices had to come since a few days, but market sentiment remains firm," said Ajit Sanghvi of Malini Ajit Sanghvi, member-brokers of the Bombay Stock Exchange.
Players said the market had discounted an impending hike in prices of petroleum products which the United Front's Steering Committee will tackle at a meeting at 1700 hours on Monday.
But India's main communist parties, partners in the coalition government said they would reiterate their opposition to any proposal to raise petroleum product prices.
"We are still opposing the increases. We have not changed our stance," Sitaram Yechury, a leader of the Communist Party of India (CPI) and a member of the Steering Committee, told Reuters.

By the end of March, domestic oil firms were owed 155 billion rupees ($4.3 billion) from the oil pool account deficit, which represents the amount owed by the government to the companies for selling below market prices.
-- Anshuman Daga, Bombay equities desk +91-22-265 9000
